title: BUCKLAND AND FAMILY v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary: In the case of Buckland and Family v. the United Kingdom, the applicants were Ms. Buckland, her immediate and extended family, all of whom identified as Romany Gypsies—a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The core issue concerned the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing obstacles to maintaining their traditional nomadic lifestyle and securing stable accommodation, particularly when local planning laws restrict their ability to settle on their own land. In October 1993, Ms. Buckland and her sister purchased a plot known as the Paddock in Tanworth in Arden, Warwickshire, aiming to provide a permanent base for their families, especially to support the education and health needs of their children, including a terminally ill daughter. After moving onto the land in April 1994, the local authority served an enforcement notice requiring the removal of their caravans due to lack of planning permission. Despite appeals highlighting their cultural, medical, and educational needs, the planning inspector rejected their case in March 1996, citing environmental and safety concerns. The applicants alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). However, following the European Court’s judgment in the related Buckley v. the United Kingdom case, which found no violation, the applicants withdrew their complaint, and the Commission struck the case out. This case illustrates the persistent legal and practical barriers faced by Roma and Traveller families in securing accommodation, a challenge rooted in longstanding patterns of exclusion across Europe.
